raw.rationale: A fixed 50-element stack buffer `wchar_t dest[50]` is filled with `wcsncpy(dest, data, wcslen(data))`; the copy length is derived entirely from the attacker-controlled input string `data`, so any input of length >= 50 writes past the end of `dest`, and the subsequent `dest[50-1] = L'\0'` only nulls the last in-bounds element, offering no bounds protection. This is a stack-based out-of-bounds write.

The destructor copies strlen(data) bytes (99, as set by the constructor) into a 50-byte stack buffer `dest` via memmove, overflowing the stack frame (CWE-787 out-of-bounds write). The subsequent `delete [] data` mismatches the `char *` allocation form, adding further memory-safety problems.

The statement `strcpy(dest, data);` copies a NUL-terminated string of attacker-controlled, unbounded length (`data = dataArray[2]`) into the fixed 50-byte stack array `char dest[50]`. No length check, no bounded copy (strncpy/memcpy with size) is performed, so any source longer than 49 bytes writes past the end of `dest`, smashing the stack (saved registers/return address). This is a concrete stack-based buffer overflow with a direct trigger.

wcscpy(dest, data) copies the 99-character wide string in data (100-element heap buffer with 99 'A' plus terminator) into dest, a 50-element stack array, overwriting past its end and smashing the stack frame (CWE-787 out-of-bounds write / CWE-120 classic stack buffer overflow). The copy length is attacker-independent but fixed at 99 wchar_t into a 50 wchar_t buffer, so the overflow is unconditional and reachable from the unconditional call at the end of the file.

The loop at line 34-37 writes 100 ints (400 bytes) into `data`, a raw pointer received from the caller via `myStruct.structFirst` (line 28), with no check of the actual allocation size. The source array `source[100]` is a local 400-byte stack buffer, so the write side is always in-bounds, but the destination is an unbounded heap pointer: any allocation smaller than 100 ints overflows the heap at `data[i] = source[i];` (line 36), giving a heap-based out-of-bounds write with attacker-influenced adjacent-heap corruption.

In sym_b21dee(), the statement `int64_t result = data * data;` performs an unchecked signed 64-bit multiplication of a value taken directly from the caller-supplied dataVector[2] with itself. For any |data| > 2^31 (e.g. values near INT64_MAX or below -2^32) the product exceeds the representable range of int64_t, producing signed integer overflow / undefined behavior and a silently wrong value that is then consumed by printLongLongLine(). No range validation or saturating/unsigned arithmetic guards the operation, so attacker-controlled vector contents can trigger the overflow.

sym_f4c2ee() copies 11 wchar_t (SRC_STRING "AAAAAAAAAA" plus NUL, i.e. (wcslen(source)+1)*sizeof(wchar_t) = 22 bytes) into the caller-supplied pointer `data` with memcpy() after only a stack-local `source[10+1]` array is built; the function performs no size/null validation of `data`, so the write is an out-of-bounds heap/stack write whenever the destination buffer is smaller than 11 wchar_t (the concrete defective statement is the memcpy into the unvalidated parameter `data`).

sym_b21dee copies the attacker-reachable wide string `source` into the destination pointer `data` (obtained from the caller) with `wcsncpy(data, source, wcslen(source) + 1)` and never checks the allocated size of `data`, so a destination buffer smaller than 11 wchar_t units is overflowed and the result is later passed to printWLine and freed.

sym_7a44aa() performs a fixed-length, unchecked write into a caller-supplied buffer: `wmemset(data, L'A', 100-1)` followed by `data[100-1] = L'\0'` writes 100 wchar_t (400 bytes on 32-bit wchar_t) into `data`, while the function takes no length/size argument and performs no capacity check. Under the `#ifndef OMITBAD` guard this is the deliberately-unsafe 'bad' variant, and any caller passing a buffer smaller than 100 wide characters suffers an out-of-bounds write.

`wcscpy(data, source)` copies 100 wchar_t (99 'C' chars plus terminator, set at source[100-1]) into `data`, a pointer taken from dataVector[2] whose allocated size is never checked or bounded by the 100-element local source; any allocation smaller than 100 wchar_t is written past its end, an out-of-bounds heap write. The subsequent `delete [] data` additionally frees a block whose allocation type/size are unverified (mismatched deallocation).

Network-supplied data is parsed with atoi() into the int `data` in sym_0dd2c9 with no range validation, and that tainted value is then incremented and used in sym_b21dee (`data++; int result = data;`). An attacker who connects to the listening socket and sends a string such as "2147483647" or "99999999999999999999" drives atoi() past INT_MAX (undefined behavior, CWE-190) and produces a signed overflow in `data++`. The stack buffer itself is handled correctly (recv() limited to CHAR_ARRAY_SIZE-1 with CHAR_ARRAY_SIZE = 3*sizeof(int)+2 = 14, and inputBuffer[recvResult] stays in bounds), so the only defective statement is the unvalidated attacker-controlled integer arithmetic.

Inside the loop `for (i = 0; i < dataLen; i++)` the statement `dest[i] = data[i];` copies the full length of the attacker-controlled input string into a fixed 50-byte stack buffer with no bounds check, so any input longer than 49 bytes overwrites past the end of `dest[50]` (the later `dest[50-1] = '\0';` only clamps the terminator and does not bound the copy loop), producing a stack-based out-of-bounds write.

In sym_26cfe9() the local `data` is set to CHAR_MAX (127) and the guard `if(data > 0)` only checks sign, so the statement `char result = data * 2;` multiplies 127 by 2 producing 254, a value outside the range of the destination type `char` (max 127 for signed char, max 255 for unsigned). The narrowing conversion of an out-of-range value to `char` yields an implementation-defined/truncated result, silently corrupting the value written to `result` and consumed by printHexCharLine(); the data>0 check is insufficient to prevent the overflow. This is a CWE-190 arithmetic/truncation overflow with a concrete triggering path (CHAR_MAX branch then data>0 branch).

The function allocates a buffer of exactly 10 wchar_t elements (`data = (wchar_t *)malloc(10*sizeof(wchar_t));`) while the file's own SRC_STRING is a 10-character wide string that requires 11 elements (10 chars + L'\0'); the resulting undersized buffer returned through the reference parameter `data` causes a one-element out-of-bounds write on any subsequent copy of SRC_STRING into it.

sym_b21dee() takes a short read from an attacker-influenced vector and computes `short result = data + 1;`; when data == 32767 the incremented value exceeds the range of the destination type and is narrowed back into `short`, producing an out-of-range/wrapped value (integer overflow / wraparound) that the program then propagates and prints. This is the classic signed-integer overflow-and-truncation defect (CWE-190/CWE-197) with no bounds check or range validation on the untrusted short before the arithmetic.

The statement strcat(data, source) appends 99 'C' bytes plus a terminating NUL onto the pointer `data` taken from dataArray[2] with no knowledge of its allocated size and no NULL/termination check; if the destination buffer is smaller than 100 bytes this writes past the end of the allocation, a heap/buffer overflow (also undefined behavior if `data` is not NUL-terminated).

sym_7e24f1() mixes narrow and wide string semantics on the same object: dataLen is computed with strlen((char *)data) (byte length of a char buffer), the destination is sized as calloc(dataLen+1, sizeof(wchar_t)), and then the copy is performed with wcscpy(dest, data), which treats the same pointer as a wchar_t* and copies until a 4-byte-aligned zero. If data is a narrow (char) string, wcscpy scans 4 bytes at a time and will read up to 3 bytes past the end of the char allocation and keep scanning unallocated heap until it happens to find a 4-zero-byte pattern - an out-of-bounds heap read (the data is also never checked for NULL before strlen, so a NULL return from sym_373045 crashes in strlen). If data is in fact a wide string, strlen() counts only up to the first zero byte of the first wchar_t, undercounting the true length, and wcscpy then writes far more wchar_t elements than the (dataLen+1) allocation can hold - a heap buffer overflow. Either branch is a memory-safety defect caused by the char/wchar_t type confusion at the wcscpy/strlen pairing.

The constructor allocates `data = (wchar_t *)malloc(50*sizeof(wchar_t))` (200 bytes where wchar_t is 4 bytes, 50 elements), but the destructor builds `wchar_t source[100]` with `wmemset(source, L'C', 100-1)` and `wcscpy(data, source)` copies up to 100 wchar_t (400 bytes on Linux) into the 50-element heap buffer, overflowing the allocation by ~200 bytes (CWE-787). The `data = dataCopy` assignment is also immediately overwritten, leaking the caller's buffer, but the wcscpy out-of-bounds write is the concrete defect.

In sym_b520e7::action, strcat(data, source) appends the 100-byte string `source` (99 'C' chars plus terminator) onto the caller-supplied `data` buffer without any bounds check or remaining-capacity check, overflowing the destination heap buffer (CWE-120/CWE-787 out-of-bounds write). The subsequent printLine(data) also reads past the buffer end, and `delete[] data` frees a buffer whose content is already corrupted.

Stack buffer overflow: `wchar_t dest[50]` is filled by `wcsncpy(dest, data, wcslen(data))`, where the copy length comes from the attacker/data-controlled string `data` rather than from the size of `dest`. Any `data` string of 50 or more wide characters (including the 50-element heap buffer at sym_7031ae) writes past the end of the 50-element stack array, corrupting the stack; the trailing `dest[50-1] = L'\0'` occurs only after the overflowing copy.

In sym_1902e3(), `strncat(dest, data, strlen(data))` on a 50-byte `dest` is bounded by the length of the unterminated/oversized source `data` (a 100-byte buffer filled with 100 non-NUL characters by sym_052df0), not by the 49 bytes of space remaining in dest. The call therefore writes 100 bytes plus a NUL past the end of the 50-byte stack buffer; the subsequent `dest[50-1] = '\0'` only writes back inside the buffer and cannot prevent the earlier out-of-bounds write.

In sym_ce02c2, the statement `short result = data * 2;` narrows the int-promoted product back into a 16-bit signed type while `data` may be any positive short up to 32767; for data >= 16384 the value 2*data exceeds SHRT_MAX and the narrowing conversion is out of range (undefined/implementation-defined signed overflow, CWE-190) producing a wrong, possibly negative result that is then consumed by printIntLine. No bounds check such as `data <= SHRT_MAX/2` guards the multiplication.

sym_ed9599 dereferences a caller-supplied `int *dataPtr` and performs `memmove(data, source, 10*sizeof(int))` - a fixed 40-byte copy into a heap buffer whose size is never validated or known inside the function, so any allocation smaller than 10 ints yields an out-of-bounds heap write; the subsequent `printIntLine(data[0])` and `free(data)` additionally read from and release memory this function does not own.

sym_5b5fb3 unconditionally copies a 99-wchar_t NUL-terminated buffer into the caller-supplied 'data' pointer via wcscpy(data, source) with no check that data has room for 100 wchar_t elements; if the caller's allocation is smaller, wcscpy writes out of bounds (CWE-120/CWE-787). The trailing free(data) further implies data is a heap buffer whose size is not tracked here.

The statement `int result = data * square` in sym_ed4800::action multiplies two attacker/caller-controlled signed ints and stores the result in a signed int; when data is large (e.g. 46341 or larger in magnitude, or any value whose square exceeds INT_MAX) the multiplication overflows a signed integer, which is undefined behavior and yields a wrong/garbage value that is then propagated by printIntLine. No range check, no unsigned/saturating arithmetic, and no guard exists anywhere in the function.

In sym_b21dee(), the statement memmove(dest, data, strlen(data)*sizeof(char)) copies an attacker-controlled length (strlen(data)) into a fixed 50-byte stack buffer dest[50] initialized only as an empty string; if data holds more than 50 bytes, the copy writes past the end of dest, an out-of-bounds stack write. The subsequent dest[50-1] = '\0' does not prevent the earlier overflow.

sym_2d7cbe writes 100 int64_t elements through data (obtained from myStruct.structFirst) into a heap buffer whose allocated size is never checked: the loop `for (i = 0; i < 100; i++) { data[i] = source[i]; }` performs a fixed-count 800-byte write to an externally supplied, unvalidated pointer, which is an out-of-bounds heap write (CWE-122) whenever data was allocated for fewer than 100 elements.

strcpy(data, source) at line 41 copies the fixed 11-byte literal source (source[10+1]) into the caller-supplied buffer `data` (obtained by dereferencing the void* parameter) with no length validation of the destination, producing an unbounded write/out-of-bounds copy; the subsequent printLine(data) also reads past any truncated/overflowed region, and the buffer is then deleted as if it were a heap array.

`++data;` preincrements a `short` (line ~32) whose value originates from the incoming struct member `myStruct.structFirst`. The module is named for the `short_max` case, i.e. the function is invoked with `structFirst == SHRT_MAX`, so `++data` performs a signed addition of 1 to a value at the maximum representable `short`, which is signed integer overflow and therefore undefined behaviour (CWE-190). The overflowed result is then narrowed/used as `short result = data;` and printed, so the tainted wrapped value propagates to the output. No bounds check or saturating logic guards the increment, so the defective statement is the unchecked preincrement itself.

In the destructor, `short result = data + 1;` takes a user-controlled `short` member (populated by `fscanf(stdin, "%hd", &data)`) and adds 1, then stores the widened int result back into a 16-bit `short`. The conversion is out of range for any `data == 32767` (e.g. input "32767"), so the value wraps/truncates in an implementation-defined manner, silently corrupting the printed result. This is a concrete, input-reachable integer overflow/truncation defect rather than a style issue.

The destructor performs `unsigned int result = data * data;` on a value read from attacker-controlled input (`fscanf(stdin, "%u", &data)`) with no range check; the multiplication can wrap around modulo 2^32, so the computed/printed value does not represent the true square. This is an integer overflow (CWE-190) that silently changes the result used for the subsequent printUnsignedLine, i.e. a wrong-value computation driven by untrusted input. Note the impact is limited: the result is only printed, not used for allocation/indexing/memory access, so no memory-safety or injection consequence is directly reachable in this file.

sym_d6c827() allocates data = (wchar_t *)malloc(10*sizeof(wchar_t)) (only 10 wchar_t / 20 bytes) and then hands the buffer to sym_402c1e(), whose purpose is to store the fixed string SRC_STRING L"AAAAAAAAAA". That string needs 11 wchar_t (10 characters plus the terminating wide NUL), so the destination is one element short: the copy performed by sym_402c1e() writes 2 bytes past the end of the 20-byte heap allocation. The undersized allocation statement `data = (wchar_t *)malloc(10*sizeof(wchar_t));` is the defective statement (CWE-131 incorrect buffer size calculation leading to CWE-787 out-of-bounds heap write). The buffer is also never freed, but that is secondary.

The overwritten voidSecond is then passed to printLine((char *)structCharVoid->voidSecond), i.e. a corrupted pointer built from string bytes is dereferenced.

In sym_a1f8ec, strncpy(dest, data, strlen(data)) copies strlen(data) bytes into the fixed 50-byte stack buffer dest. The bound is derived from the attacker/user-controlled input length rather than the destination size, so any data longer than 50 bytes writes past the end of dest (stack out-of-bounds write); the trailing dest[50-1]='\0' only mitigates the missing-NUL case, not the overflow. This is a classic off-by-size copy loop in a juliet-style CWE-121/CWE-787 test case.

The statement `wcsncpy(dest, data, wcslen(data))` copies wcslen(data) wide characters into `wchar_t dest[50]`, a 50-element stack buffer, with no bound on the count against the destination size. Since the length argument is derived from the source string (returned by the out-of-line sym_052df0() and therefore not known to fit), any data longer than 49 characters causes wcsncpy to write past the end of dest, corrupting the stack; the following `dest[50-1] = L'\0'` does not mitigate the already-performed out-of-bounds write. This is an out-of-bounds write (stack buffer overflow).
In sym_1902e3, `data = new char[50]` allocates 50 bytes, but the code then copies 100 bytes into it and writes `data[100-1] = '\0'`, a 50-byte heap buffer overflow.

sym_b21dee performs strcat(data, source) where `source` holds 99 non-null bytes plus terminator, appending a fixed ~99-byte payload into `data`, a heap buffer obtained from dataList.back() whose size is nowhere validated in this function and which is later free()d. There is no length check, bounds computation, or reallocation before the unbounded concatenation, so a destination allocated at or near the 100-byte region is overwritten past its bounds, producing a heap-based buffer overflow.

The call `SNPRINTF(dest, strlen(data), "%s", data)` passes the *source* string length as the destination bound instead of `sizeof(dest)` (50). The output is therefore always truncated by one byte, and when `strlen(data) == 0` a size of 0 is passed, which is invalid/negative for the Windows `_snprintf` branch (which also does not guarantee NUL-termination and can write past the supplied count on non-conformant legacy implementations). The correct size argument is the capacity of `dest`, so this statement is a defective buffer-size calculation.

sym_052df0() writes a fixed 100 bytes into the caller-supplied `data` pointer without any length parameter or size validation: `memset(data, 'A', 100-1);` followed by `data[100-1] = '\0';`. Any buffer smaller than 100 bytes is overflowed by this unconditional store sequence, so the function has no safe calling contract and is a concrete out-of-bounds write.

In sym_56fb4e() the stack buffer `char dest[50]` is only 50 bytes, but the bound passed to strncat is `strlen(data)`, which is 99 in the first branch (data is filled with 99 'A' bytes plus a NUL). `strncat(dest, data, strlen(data))` therefore appends 99 characters plus a terminating NUL into a 50-byte buffer, writing 100 bytes onto the stack. The subsequent `dest[50-1] = '\0';` only overwrites one byte of the overflow and does not prevent it. This is a stack-based out-of-bounds write.

sym_618110() copies 100 bytes into the caller-supplied buffer `data` via `data[i] = source[i];` for i in [0,100) and then writes the terminator at `data[100-1]`, without ever allocating or validating the size of `data`. The function treats `data` as at least 100 bytes and additionally calls `free(data)` on it, so the contract it relies on (a >=100-byte heap allocation) is entirely external and unverified here; any caller supplying a smaller allocation gets a 100-byte out-of-bounds heap write. This is the classic fixed-size-buffer copy sink whose size is not established in the function that writes it.

sym_2ee4f3() writes a fixed 40-byte block (10*sizeof(int)) into the caller-supplied pointer `data` via memcpy without any check that the destination holds at least 10 ints; the subsequent printIntLine(data[0]) and free(data) also assume the full extent is valid. If the caller passes a buffer smaller than 40 bytes this is an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787/CWE-120); the defective statement is the memcpy into an unchecked external pointer.

The function copies a fixed 100 wchar_t (400 bytes) block into `data`, a heap pointer taken from `dataList.back()` whose allocated size is never established in this file, and then writes `data[100-1] = L'\0'`. The `memcpy(data, source, 100*sizeof(wchar_t))` statement performs a fixed-length out-of-bounds heap write whenever the caller's buffer is smaller than 100 wchar_t elements (the buffer provenance/size is entirely external to the file), and the subsequent indexing plus `delete [] data` assume ownership of a buffer of unknown allocation, which is also a potential mismatched-delete. This is the classic unvalidated-destination-length heap copy defect.

The constructor reads up to CHAR_ARRAY_SIZE-1 (14-1=13) bytes from a socket into inputBuffer and stores atoi(inputBuffer) into member `data` (line ~91), with no upper-bound validation. The destructor then allocates a fixed 10-int heap buffer and, guarded only by the check `if (data >= 0)`, executes `buffer[data] = 1;` (line ~122). A server response such as "999999999" makes data a large positive value, producing an attacker-controlled out-of-bounds heap write far past the 40-byte allocation, corrupting heap metadata and adjacent memory.

In sym_35614e, the statement `data++` increments a `char` parameter with no range check, so a call with data == CHAR_MAX causes signed integer overflow (undefined behavior) when stored back into the char; the sibling function sym_c6fa0e demonstrates the correct guarded pattern, confirming this is a defect.

In sym_398410, `wcsncpy(dest, data, wcslen(data))` copies exactly strlen(data) wide characters into the fixed 50-element stack array `dest` with no bound on the source length; if `data` is 50 or more wchar_t long, the write overruns `dest[50]`. The subsequent `dest[50-1] = L'\0'` does not prevent the overflow because the out-of-bounds write has already occurred. The length argument should be bounded (e.g. `wcsncpy(dest, data, 50-1)`).

In sym_5a39d3(), a fixed 50-wchar_t stack buffer `dest` is concatenated with the caller-supplied `data` via `wcscat(dest, data)` with no length validation of `data`, so any `data` of 49 wchar_t or more (or with no NUL terminator) overflows the stack buffer; the following printWLine(data) also reads out of bounds. No bound on `data` is established anywhere in the file.

In sym_398410, `int result = data + 1;` is computed on a value read from the caller-supplied dataVector with no upper-bound check, so an attacker-controlled data == INT_MAX causes signed integer overflow (undefined behavior, wraparound). The sibling function sym_611203 demonstrates the required `if (data < INT_MAX)` guard is missing here.

In sym_2ee8fa the statement `char result = data * 2;` is executed whenever `data > 0` with no upper bound, so for any data > CHAR_MAX/2 (e.g. data = 100) the multiplication overflows the signed char conversion range, producing undefined behavior and a corrupted value. The companion function sym_b001bf in the same file shows the intended fix (`if (data < (CHAR_MAX/2))`), confirming the missing bound in sym_2ee8fa is the defect rather than intentional behavior.

In sym_398410, memmove(dest, data, strlen(data)*sizeof(char)) copies an attacker-influenced length into a fixed 50-byte stack buffer with no check that strlen(data) < 50, so any input of 50 bytes or more overflows the stack buffer (the following dest[49]='\0' only clamps the terminator after the overflow already occurred).

strcat(dest, data) appends the unbounded externally-supplied string dataArray[2] into a fixed 50-byte stack buffer `char dest[50] = "";` with no length check, so any input longer than 49 bytes (the usual testcase supplies 100+ bytes) writes past the end of the stack buffer, corrupting the stack.

The constructor first assigns the caller-owned buffer to the member pointer (`data = dataCopy;`) and then unconditionally overwrites that pointer with a fresh `malloc(100*sizeof(wchar_t))` block, so the buffer referenced by dataCopy is orphaned and never released (the destructor only `free(data)`, i.e. the new block). This is a concrete missing-release defect (CWE-401) with a leak on every object construction; no OOB write/overflow exists, so severity is limited to resource exhaustion.

In sym_1902e3(), data is set to NULL and passed by reference to sym_052df0(char * &data), whose result is never checked before `strncat(data, source, 100)` and `printLine(data)`; if the callee fails to allocate (or is compiled such that it leaves data NULL), the strncat dereferences a NULL pointer. The missing NULL/return-value check on the allocation is the defective statement path.

`char * data = dataMap[2];` uses the non-const `std::map::operator[]` on the by-value parameter, which default-inserts a NULL entry for a missing key 2, and in any case yields a heap pointer whose allocation size is never known or validated. The subsequent `SNPRINTF(data, 100, "%s", source);` (file:51) then writes up to 100 bytes into that unverified buffer (99 'C' bytes plus terminator), so if the caller's buffer is smaller than 100 bytes this is a heap out-of-bounds write, and if key 2 is absent `data` is NULL and the call is a null-pointer write. There is no size/bounds check between acquisition and the fixed-size-100 write.

sym_398410 allocates a fixed heap buffer of 10 ints (`int * buffer = new int[10];`) and then guards the write with only `if (data >= 0)`. Any non-negative `data` >= 10 passes the check and executes `buffer[data] = 1;`, an out-of-bounds heap write with attacker-controlled offset and no upper-bound check (contrast with the correctly bounded sibling function sym_611203, which tests `data >= 0 && data < (10)`). This is a concrete, demonstrable heap buffer overflow primitive.

In sym_8b3f6c() the pointer `data` is taken from the never-assigned global `sym_64284c` and used without any NULL check or validation of the pointee's size; `memmove(data, source, 100*sizeof(twoIntsStruct))` then unconditionally writes 100 struct elements into that untrusted/uninitialized target, followed by printStructLine(&data[0]) and free(data). If the global is NULL or points to a smaller/foreign object, this is a NULL/wild-pointer write of 800+ bytes (and an invalid free), a concrete memory-safety defect with a direct triggering path.

In sym_fb0f4e(), the local pointer `data` is initialized to NULL and passed to sym_470857(); the return value is used unconditionally, so when sym_470857() returns the NULL input (the expected path in this test case), the statement `strncpy(data, source, strlen(source) + 1);` writes through a NULL pointer (subsequently printLine(data) and free(data) also dereference it), an unconditional NULL pointer dereference.

In sym_438f52, the statement `int64_t result = data * data;` multiplies an attacker-controlled int64_t with no bound or overflow check, so any |data| > 3037000499 wraps/triggers signed overflow (undefined behavior), corrupting the value that is then used. The sibling function sym_521d65 demonstrates the intended guard (imaxabs(data) <= sqrtl(LLONG_MAX)), confirming the missing check in sym_438f52 is the defect.

strncat(dest, data, strlen(data)) with dest[50] = "" is not a bounded copy: strncat always appends the full n source characters plus a terminating NUL, so it writes strlen(data)+1 bytes into a 50-byte stack buffer. When the attacker-supplied 'data' string is 50 bytes or longer, the terminating NUL (and the 50th data byte) is written past dest[49], corrupting the stack; the following dest[50-1]='\0' write does not prevent the overflow because it occurs after the damage.

sym_b21dee() takes list<char> dataList by value and immediately calls dataList.back() without verifying the container is non-empty; for std::list, back() dereferences the last node, and invoking it on an empty list dereferences the sentinel/end node, which is undefined behavior (out-of-bounds/garbage read). The value read is then used in an arithmetic expression and printed, so the defect has an observable security-relevant consequence.

In the `#ifndef OMITBAD` (the intentionally-bad) variant, `sym_1902e3()` sets the local pointer `data` to NULL and immediately passes it to `sym_9c10d3(data)`, handing a null pointer to a function that consumes it. This is the canonical uninitialized/NULL-dereference trigger: any access to the pointee in the callee faults. The defect is the deliberate `data = NULL;` followed by dereference-prone use at the call site, guarded so the null is only passed in the non-OMITBAD build.

sym_af9da1() performs `char result = data * data;` on a caller-supplied `char data` with no magnitude guard, unlike the sibling functions sym_0bedf5/sym_37b994 which clamp with `abs((long)data) <= (long)sqrt((double)CHAR_MAX)` before the same multiplication. For any |data| > 11 (e.g. data = 127) the int product reaches 16129, which does not fit in char; the assignment silently narrows/truncates the value (implementation-defined for signed char, wrapping/overflow of the destination type), so the value subsequently passed to printHexCharLine is not the computed quantity. The defective statement is the unguarded narrowing multiplication in sym_af9da1.

In sym_dd96c8 the index `data` is only validated for being non-negative before `buffer[data] = 1;` is executed on a heap buffer of 10 ints allocated with `new int[10]`, so any value >= 10 writes out of bounds (heap buffer overflow). The sibling function sym_145891 shows the intended guard (`data >= 0 && data < 10`) that is missing here, confirming the missing upper-bound check is a defect rather than an intentional design.

sym_3382eb/sym_3380eb performs an unchecked increment of the signed int parameter `data++` (sample.c:82) with no `data < INT_MAX` guard, unlike the sibling functions sym_2312d7 (line 45) and sym_58ce53 (line 64) which do guard it. If the caller supplies INT_MAX, the increment overflows a signed int (undefined behavior / CWE-190) and the wrapped value is consumed in `int result = data; printIntLine(result);`.

Any input longer than 50 bytes overflows the stack buffer (the trailing `dest[50-1] = '\0'` occurs only after the already-corrupting copy). This is a stack-based out-of-bounds write. Additionally, `delete [] data` frees memory owned by the caller's struct (potential mismatched/foreign free), and the copy omits the NUL terminator.

In sym_02d94c(), the statement `++data;` performs an unchecked increment on a signed int whose value is fully attacker-controlled via dataArray[2], with no `data < INT_MAX` guard; when data == INT_MAX this is signed integer overflow (undefined behavior) and wraps to INT_MIN, propagating a corrupted value into `result`. The adjacent sym_ca1956() shows the intended guard, confirming the omission is a defect rather than design.

The incremented value is then propagated into `result` and consumed downstream, so a downstream size/index computation based on it can wrap to a small value.

The defective statement is `data = (int *)malloc(50*sizeof(int));` in sym_ad1b21(): the function overwrites its incoming `int *data` parameter with a fresh allocation before any use, permanently discarding the caller's pointer, so the original heap block is leaked and can never be freed. No other memory-safety or overflow issue is present (the size expression 50*sizeof(int) is constant and non-overflowing).

`delete [] data;` is applied to a variable of static type `wchar_t *` (a pointer to a non-array type), not to a `wchar_t[]`; invoking array-deallocation on a non-array pointer is undefined behavior and results in a mismatched deallocator (heap corruption / invalid free) depending on how the source buffer was obtained. Separately, the `memmove(dest, data, wcslen(data)*sizeof(wchar_t))` into the 50-element stack buffer has no clamp on the source length, so any source of 50 or more wide characters writes past `dest` (stack out-of-bounds write).

The callee obtains a raw pointer from a container (`int * data = dataList.back();`) and then releases it with the C allocator (`free(data);`) even though the pointer's ownership/provenance is a C++ object inside `dataList` (a copy of the caller's list). Nothing in the function establishes that the pointee came from malloc, and the list (both the caller's and the by-value copy) still references the freed object, so `free(data)` is a mismatched/invalid deallocation leaving a dangling pointer that can be released or dereferenced again. Additionally, `memcpy(data, source, 10*sizeof(int))` writes 40 bytes into a pointer whose allocated size is not established anywhere in this function, so an undersized `data` target is a heap overflow.

In sym_82e8a3() the statement `unsigned int result = data * 2;` multiplies an externally supplied unsigned int (sym_585525) by 2 with no bound check, so values above UINT_MAX/2 wrap around. In sym_6091b4(), 'short result = data * data;' multiplies an attacker-supplied 'short' without the bounds check present in the companion function sym_d87e3f(). A large 'data' (e.g. 30000) yields a product (900,000,000 range, up to 1,073,676,289) far beyond SHRT_MAX, so the int-to-short narrowing assignment is an unchecked integer overflow / out-of-range conversion whose result is used and printed, the classic CWE-190 defect the guarded variant fixes.

In sym_cbb79d the write `buffer[data] = 1;` is guarded only by `if (data >= 0)`, with no upper-bound check against the 10-element buffer, so any attacker-influenced `data` value of 10 or greater produces an out-of-bounds heap write (heap buffer overflow), unlike the sibling function sym_7df8fa which correctly bounds it with `data < 10`.

In sym_80b2a0() the statement `int64_t result = data * data;` multiplies two attacker-influenced int64_t values from dataArray[2] with no range check, so values with |data| > sqrt(LLONG_MAX) overflow the signed type. This is a classic out-of-bounds write (off-by-cap count) in an unbounded strncat.

sym_501ce1() writes an externally supplied, unvalidated heap pointer with a fixed-length copy: `memcpy(data, source, (strlen(source) + 1) * sizeof(char))` writes 11 bytes into `data = myStruct.structFirst`, whose allocated size is never established or checked in this function before the copy. The correct size argument is 50 (or sizeof(dest)/sizeof(wchar_t)), and even the source-length form omits the byte for the terminator.

sym_c42654 receives the pointer `data` as a by-value parameter and unconditionally applies array delete `delete [] data`; the callee never allocated that buffer with `new[]`, so the deallocation is a mismatched/undefined free (and would be a mismatched deallocator if the caller used malloc/new int64_t), which is a concrete defect independent of the caller. No other statement in the file can release the allocation, so the leak is concretely and deterministically reachable.
